hook: The Crocker Bank Building of 1908, an Article 10 landmark, at the address where Japanese merchants took a store in 1871.

parcel.note: Business addresses are usually deferred on this site; this page exists because the address was named in the prompting source. The parcel carries the two-storey banking hall only — the 38-storey tower behind it on the same block is a separate parcel (0292004, 68–82 Post Street), though DBI files its permits under this address.

historic_status.reason: Article 10 Individual Landmark, Historic Resource Evaluation Response, Historic Survey Result

historic_district.note: The parcel's coordinates fall inside no historic district; its protection is the individual Article 10 designation.

permits.description: revision to the February 2020 permit, to remove the vaults in the basement
selective interior demolition of finishes and partitions in the basement and on the second floor, with the structure, the exterior and the historic features to remain

ground floor and mezzanine — heating and ventilation remodelled with new duct distribution, three fan coil units, two rooftop condensing units and a new mechanical room on the mezzanine, with lighting revisions and structural support for the plant

permits_note: Three of the 792 filings under this address and parcel are shown. DBI files work in the neighbouring 38-storey office tower under the same address, so only filings whose description identifies the two-storey banking hall — its basement vaults, its mezzanine, its historic features — are listed here.

historical_record.summary: Japanese mercantile firm takes a store
historical_record.description: Men who had come with Japan's contribution to the Mechanics' Institute fair of 1871 stayed in San Francisco as permanent residents and set up a mercantile firm, leasing a store in the Masonic Temple at 1 Montgomery Street.

historical_record.summary: What the firm would trade in
historical_record.description: The firm would deal in the staple products of Japan — tea, coal, flax and wax — rather than knick-knacks, and had the means to do business on a large scale, the Bulletin reported.
